title: foreman-mcp-server -- T1563 session-ID logged + never re-validated enables hijacking
author: WinstonRedGuard -- sigma plugin observed rules (derived from breach corpus)
description:
Vendor-disclosed detection for CVE-2026-12112, a Red Hat security
advisory (Bugzilla 2488031, RHSA-2026:28405 / RHSA-2026:28438) for the
foreman-mcp-server MCP server.

The server caches the fully-authenticated Foreman API client connection
object in an in-memory dictionary (`user_map`), keyed by the
`mcp-session-id` -- which the advisory states plainly is NOT a secret.
Two compounding facts make this exploitable rather than merely sloppy:
(1) the server logs every newly-created session ID at INFO level (the
advisory's own classification: "F-32 MCP Server: Insecure Sensitive HTTP
Header Sanitization"), so a session ID that should function like a
credential ends up in ordinary application logs; (2) although the
`foreman_token` header is required to establish a session, it is NEVER
RE-VALIDATED on subsequent requests -- once a session ID is known, any
caller presenting it (with any token value, or none) is served through
the cached, already-authenticated connection. An attacker who reads a
legitimate session ID out of application logs can hijack that user's
authenticated Foreman session indefinitely, no valid token required
after the first request.

Detection logic flags the disclosure half of this chain, since it is the
half a log source can actually observe: an `mcp-session-id` value
appearing in an application log line at INFO level. This is
deliberately NOT a claim that every such log line is an active attack --
the vulnerability is systemic on an unpatched install (every session
creation logs its ID by design), so this rule's honest scope is "is this
deployment still exposing session IDs the way the advisory describes",
not "here is a confirmed hijacking in progress" -- stated in
falsepositives rather than implied.

Aggregated from 1 first-party vendor security advisory (Red Hat, via
Bugzilla and the linked RHSA errata).
